rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.4 describe a greenhouse experiment with two drip-irrigation treatments (T1 drinking water + full fertilization; T2 treated wastewater + partial fertilization), four plots each, two lettuce cycles. Q2: Section 3.3 and Table 6 report that fresh weight of lettuce under T2 (TWW drip with partial fertilization) was significantly larger than under T1, 48% larger in cycle 1 and 100% larger in cycle 2. Q4: Table 1 quantifies the nutrient content of the TWW (N, P, K, Ca at least 200% higher than drinking water), Table 3 reports soil nutrients after each cycle and Table 5 reports leaf nutrient concentrations; authors attribute the yield gain to continuous nutrient supply by TWW during the whole cycle. Q8: Conclusions state that evaluation of crops with longer cycles and more repetitions is recommended and that field research under the same conditions is encouraged (i.e., greenhouse, short-cycle crop, few repetitions). Q9: Table 6 gives MSD and CV% for fresh weight for each cycle (CV 16.4% and 29.1%).
rows.notes: The experiment compares water source (treated wastewater vs drinking water) with drip used in both treatments; the yield result is therefore evidence about TWW fertigation under drip, not about drip versus other irrigation methods. The passage itself names TSE drip irrigation, matching the study design, so Q2 is answered yes, but the row's technology field 'drip' is only loosely supported. Q3: single method (fresh-weight measurement) only. Q4: intermediate variables (water, soil and leaf nutrients) were measured, although leaf nutrient contents did not differ significantly between treatments, so the mechanism is only partly substantiated. Q7: the authors note TWW nitrogen was insufficient and had to be complemented by fertilizer, and that TWW does not replace nitrogen fertilizer, but this is partly design-based and cites other work; not clearly stated as a requirement from own findings, so rated no. Q5/Q6: one soil, one crop, one greenhouse, plot scale.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study has two cycles with four plots per treatment in a greenhouse; the authors themselves call it 'one repetition' (two cycles).
